t: Number of Valid Move Combinations On Chessboard — Enumerate Stops, Simulate Seconds
o: Up to 4 pieces (rooks, bishops, at most one queen) each choose a destination square their movement rules allow — including staying put — and then all pieces slide simultaneously one square per second along straight lines until reaching their destinations. A combination is valid iff no two pieces ever occupy the same square at the same time; note that directly adjacent pieces may legally pass through each other and swap in one second. Example 1: a corner rook can reach 14 squares plus staying — 15 combinations. Example 2: a corner queen reaches 21 squares plus staying — 22. Example 3: a bishop on (4,3) has 11 reachable diagonals plus staying — 12. Since n <= 4 and each piece has at most 57 stop choices (1 + 8 directions x up to 7 distances), enumerating every combination and validating it is entirely feasible; validation just replays the synchronized motion second by second.
k: Each move is a (direction, distance) pair with distance 0 meaning stay; n <= 4 pieces with <= 57 options each keeps brute-force enumeration tiny.
Pieces move in lockstep at one square per second, so conflicts are exactly two pieces sharing a cell at the same integer second — passing/swap events are explicitly legal.
Validation prunes early: check a newly chosen piece against already-chosen ones instead of waiting for the full assignment.

a.n: Approach 1: Backtracking over Stop Squares + Second-by-Second Simulation
a.i: Generate every legal (direction, distance) option per piece, including stay. Backtrack over all combinations; for each complete combination, simulate the synchronized advance: every second each piece steps one square toward its destination (both axes for diagonal moves), then verify all positions are pairwise distinct. The simulation ends when every piece has arrived.
s: Build per-piece option lists: (0,0,0) for stay plus every in-bounds (dr, dc, d).
Backtrack across pieces to enumerate all stop-square assignments.
For an assignment, compute destinations and replay second-by-second movement.
After each simultaneous step, reject if any two pieces share a square.
Count the assignment when all pieces reach their destinations without collision.
a.t: O(P^n x n^2 x D) worst case — P <= 57 stops per piece, n <= 4 pieces, D <= 8 simulated seconds; pruning makes this far smaller in practice.
a.sp: O(n) — recursion depth, current assignment and board positions.

a.n: Approach 2: Trajectory Comparison with Incremental Pruning
a.i: Skip the round-based loop: represent each chosen move as start, direction and duration T (Chebyshev distance to destination). Position at time t is start + direction x min(t, T) — pieces park forever after arriving. Two moves are compatible iff these time-parameterized positions differ at every integer t in [0, max T]. During backtracking, validate a candidate against only the already-chosen moves, cutting incompatible branches immediately.
s: Precompute per-piece (dr, dc, d) options as in Approach 1.
Encode a move as (start row, start col, dr, dc, T).
compatible(a, b): compare closed-form positions for t = 0..max(Ta, Tb); any equality rejects.
During backtracking accept a candidate only if compatible with every previously chosen move.
a.t: O(P^n x n^2 x D) — same family as Approach 1 but rejected branches die at the first conflicting pair instead of after full simulation.
a.sp: O(n) — recursion stack plus the current chain of chosen moves.

w: Frame the solution as enumeration + validation; either validation style passes comfortably. Pitfalls: forgetting the STAY option (distance 0), forbidding adjacent swaps (explicitly legal), moving diagonal pieces one axis per turn instead of both simultaneously, and checking collisions only at destinations rather than every second. Edge cases worth testing: single piece (answer equals its number of stop squares), two identical-direction movers that never collide, a mover landing exactly where a stationary piece sits. Follow-ups: larger boards or more pieces demand smarter pruning or meet-in-the-middle; variable speeds change only the position formula inside compatible().
